The Yellowhammer (Emberiza citrinella) is a common passerine of European farmland, and its life-history traits have been the subject of several field studies. Eggs are incubated for a period typically lasting between 12 and 14 days at an average nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]; this developmental duration yields an age at hatching of approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days], a value that aligns closely with published accounts for related bunting species. At the moment of hatching, the altricial nestlings are remarkably small, with a measured wet weight at birth of 2.7 grams [Wwb = 2.7 grams]. This modest initial mass, representing less than ten percent of the ultimate adult female body size, underscores the substantial energetic investment required during the subsequent nestling phase. The newly hatched chicks are entirely dependent on parental provisioning, and their rapid growth trajectory over the first days of life is critical for achieving the developmental milestones necessary for fledging.

Field observations indicate that female Yellowhammers reach an ultimate wet weight of 29.7 grams [Wwi = 29.7 grams] upon attaining full adulthood, a figure that places this species within the typical size range for the genus Emberiza. This asymptotic mass is achieved after a period of rapid somatic growth during the post-fledging and juvenile stages. Under the thermoneutral conditions characteristic of an active breeding adult (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), several key reproductive and developmental events are timed with notable precision. For instance, the age at which a young bird achieves its first successful flight, marking the fledging event, is recorded at 12 days after hatching [tx = 12 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This developmental pace is relatively rapid for an altricial passerine and reflects the selective pressures of a short breeding season in temperate environments, where early independence from the nest can enhance overall reproductive success.

Sexual maturation in the Yellowhammer proceeds over a somewhat longer timescale than the early developmental milestones. Under the same thermoneutral body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 36 days [tp = approximately 36 days]. It is important to note that this value represents the onset of gonadal activity and physiological readiness to breed rather than the actual initiation of nesting behavior. The gap between attaining puberty and engaging in first reproduction is often influenced by social factors, territory availability, and individual condition. In many populations, young birds may not secure a breeding territory or find a mate until several months after becoming physiologically mature. Nevertheless, the relatively early attainment of sexual maturity, when considered alongside the species' modest adult body mass of 29.7 grams [Wwi = 29.7 grams], suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes an early start to reproductive life once environmental conditions permit.

The timing of a female's first successful breeding attempt is a critical life-history parameter. In terms of annual reproductive output, females typically produce between 3 and 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 3 and 5 eggs per clutch] and may raise multiple broods within a single season. The maximum reproduction rate for the species, observed under optimal food conditions at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], involves the production of approximately 4 eggs per year, corresponding to about 1 clutch annually [F_R_i = about 1 clutch annually] given an average clutch size of 3 to 5 eggs [N_R_i = clutch size of 3 to 5 eggs], a figure that balances the energetic costs of egg formation against the demands of parental care.

Longevity records for the Yellowhammer indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 13.2 years [am = approximately 13.2 years], a value derived from ring-recovery data and sustained under typical physiological conditions at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This considerable potential lifespan, which rivals that of many larger-bodied passerines, highlights the species' capacity for sustained reproductive output over multiple seasons when environmental conditions remain favorable. The combination of a moderate adult body mass of 29.7 grams [Wwi = 29.7 grams] and a relatively long lifespan positions the Yellowhammer as an intermediate strategist on the slow-fast continuum of life-history variation. Unlike short-lived species that invest heavily in a single, large reproductive event, this bunting appears to spread its reproductive effort across many years, producing multiple clutches annually but with a relatively modest clutch size. Such a strategy is well-suited to the variable agricultural landscapes it inhabits, where food availability can fluctuate markedly between years.
